title: Becoming One with Nature
coreMove: Diagnose the system’s motion: adapt to its environment, add flywheel pushes, look for the threshold, or increase network value before expecting acceleration.
sourcePressure: The source ties natural selection, the peppered moth, flywheel momentum, tipping points, and network effects into a chapter about adaptation and self-reinforcing change.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Assuming slow progress means failure, or that momentum appears without fit, repeated pushes, thresholds, and reinforcement.

sourceAnchors.name: peppered moth example
sourceAnchors.detail: the source uses peppered moths to show fit to environment changing over time
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The moth is not stronger in the abstract; it survives because the environment has changed what “fit” means.

sourceAnchors.name: merry-go-round analogy
sourceAnchors.detail: the source uses a merry-go-round to show flywheel effort: hard to start, easier to keep moving after momentum builds
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The first push feels wasteful because the wheel has not started paying you back yet.

sourceAnchors.name: social-network example
sourceAnchors.detail: the source uses social networks to illustrate value increasing as more members join
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A network can be useless at five people and valuable at five hundred for the same reason: the members are part of the product.

exampleSpecs.domain: Grace, a coastal bookstore owner changing inventory after cruise traffic replaces local lunch-hour traffic
exampleSpecs.audience: small-business readers facing a changed environment
exampleSpecs.stakes: the old bestselling mix no longer fits the people walking in
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Grace compares the receipt stack before and after cruise season and moves portable field guides to the front table instead of blaming customers
exampleSpecs.firstImage: salt drying on the glass door below a rack of unsold hardcovers

exampleSpecs.domain: Marco, a youth soccer coach rebuilding a team’s passing rhythm with the same first drill every practice
exampleSpecs.audience: leaders frustrated by slow early momentum
exampleSpecs.stakes: parents see dull repetition before the team’s play begins to connect
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Marco keeps the five-minute rondo despite complaints, then shows how the same push starts producing faster decisions after three weeks
exampleSpecs.firstImage: cleats squeak on damp turf while the same orange cones come out again

exampleSpecs.domain: Frida, a farmers-market organizer trying to reach the stall density where shoppers browse instead of make one purchase
exampleSpecs.stakes: too few vendors make the market feel empty and self-defeating
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Frida marks the stall map and chooses to subsidize three anchor vendors because crossing the density threshold changes shopper behavior
exampleSpecs.firstImage: How many stalls make a market feel like a place instead of a table?

exampleSpecs.domain: Akira, a language-exchange host deciding whether to seed the first ten reliable participants before advertising widely
exampleSpecs.stakes: newcomers will not return if no conversation partners are present
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Akira treats the first ten members as the product, personally matches them, and only then opens public signups
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You can print a hundred flyers and still have an empty room at 7:05

exampleSpecs.domain: Rachel, a hospital volunteer coordinator recognizing that a new discharge-call program needs the ward nurses’ workflow to change first
exampleSpecs.audience: operators installing changes inside existing systems
exampleSpecs.stakes: volunteers cannot help if referrals never arrive at the right time
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Rachel traces every missed call back to the same discharge handoff and adapts the program to the nurses’ actual rhythm
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Rachel twelve missed discharge calls to stop blaming the volunteers

exampleSpecs.domain: Niklas, a maker-space treasurer deciding when monthly members are enough to justify buying a shared laser cutter
exampleSpecs.audience: club leaders balancing thresholds and reinforcement
exampleSpecs.stakes: buying too early drains dues, buying after member density arrives can accelerate retention
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Niklas waits until the waitlist and dues cross a set threshold, then shows how the cutter itself makes membership more valuable
exampleSpecs.firstImage: “If we buy it now, who uses it on Tuesday night?”

tryThisNowSpec: Name one system that feels stuck and mark which force is missing right now: fit, repeated pushes, threshold density, or reinforcement from more participants.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps
